answer:
# Memorandum — 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i): Latest Time to Rescind and Extended Expiration

**Subject:** Right of rescission, closed-end credit secured by the consumer's principal dwelling (Regulation Z, implementing TILA § 125(a)).
**Nature of opinion:** Pure question of regulatory text. No transaction facts were supplied; no transaction-specific conclusion is expressed. All quoted regulatory language below is reproduced from the five fetched sources listed in Part X, which agree verbatim.

---

## I. Questions Presented

1. Under 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), until when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction?
2. Under the same provision, when does the right expire if the required notice or the material disclosures are never delivered?

---

## II. Short Answers

**Ask 1 — latest point for exercise.** Until **midnight of the third business day** following the **last** to occur of three events: (i) consummation of the transaction; (ii) delivery of the notice of the right to rescind required by § 1026.23(b); (iii) delivery of **all** material disclosures. If the last of those three events falls on day D, the consumer may rescind at any time through the end of the third business day after D. (In a narrow class of administrative proceedings the period is extended under § 125(f) of the Act — see Part VII.A.)

**Ask 2 — expirations where notice or material disclosures are never delivered.** The right expires at the **earliest** of three events: (i) **3 years after consummation**; (ii) **transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property**; (iii) **sale of the property**. The 3-year figure is a **ceiling, not a guarantee**: a sale or a transfer of all of the consumer's interest ends the right earlier. It can never be exercised more than 3 years after consummation.

---

## III. Governing Text (quoted)

**§ 1026.23(a)(3)(i):**

> “The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act.”

**§ 1026.23(a)(3)(ii)** (what counts as “material disclosures”):

> “For the purposes of this paragraph (a)(3), the term ‘material disclosures’ means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g).”

**§ 1026.23(a)(2)** (when the consumer's notice is “given”):

> “To exercise the right to rescind, the consumer shall notify the creditor of the rescission by mail, telegram or other means of written communication. Notice is considered given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business.”

**§ 1026.23(a)(1)** (scope):

> “In a credit transaction in which a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in a consumer's principal dwelling, each consumer whose ownership interest is or will be subject to the security interest shall have the right to rescind the transaction, except for transactions described in paragraph (f) of this section. ... The creditor shall deliver the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section but need not deliver new material disclosures. Delivery of the required notice shall begin the rescission period.”

**§ 1026.23(f)** (exempt transactions) — relevant entries: **(f)(1)** a residential mortgage transaction; **(f)(2)** a refinancing or consolidation by the same creditor of credit already secured by the principal dwelling (right applies only to the extent the new amount financed exceeds the unpaid principal balance, any earned unpaid finance charge on the existing debt, and amounts attributed solely to the costs of the refinancing or consolidation); **(f)(3)** a transaction in which a state agency is a creditor; **(f)(4)** a subsequent advance in a series, where the (b) notice and all material disclosures have been given; **(f)(5)** a renewal of optional insurance premiums.

---

## IV. Analysis of Ask 1 — the Three-Event Rule

**1. Three triggers, and the last one controls.** The period does not run from consummation alone. It runs from the **last** of (a) consummation, (b) delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice, and (c) delivery of **all** material disclosures. Delivery of the notice after consummation is permitted and restarts the clock: per the official interpretation, “The notice required by § 1026.23(b) need not be given before consummation of the transaction. The creditor may deliver the notice after the transaction is consummated, but the rescission period will not begin to run until the notice is given. For example, if the creditor provides the notice on May 15, but disclosures were given and the transaction was consummated on May 10, the 3-business-day rescission period will run from May 15.”

**2. “All” material disclosures.** The clock is not started by partial disclosure. The enumerated items in (a)(3)(ii) must all be delivered: annual percentage rate, finance charge, amount financed, total of payments, payment schedule, plus the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g).

**3. Counting the three business days.** Under the official interpretation, “the period within which the consumer may exercise the right to rescind runs for 3 business days from the last of 3 events.” The day of the last triggering event is excluded, and the count runs forward over business days only. The interpretation's two illustrations:

| Facts | Expiration stated in the interpretation |
|---|---|
| Consummated Friday, June 1; disclosures and notice given Thursday, May 31 | Midnight of **Tuesday, June 5** (the third business day after June 1) |
| Disclosures given and transaction consummated Friday, June 1; rescission notice given Monday, June 4 | Midnight of **Thursday, June 7** (the third business day after June 4) |

*Counting note (important, and the one place where an arithmetic slip is likely):* in the first illustration, counting Saturday, June 2 as business day 1, Monday as 2, and Tuesday as 3 is the only way to arrive at Tuesday, June 5. The illustration therefore assumes the creditor's offices were open on the Saturday. If the creditor is closed on Saturdays, the same facts push expiration to the next business day. **Confirm the creditor's Saturday and holiday hours before relying on a specific date.** The second illustration (Tuesday 1, Wednesday 2, Thursday 3 → Thursday June 7) is unaffected.

**4. What the consumer must do by the deadline.** Not deliver — **send**. § 1026.23(a)(2): notice “is considered given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business.” The interpretation confirms: “The consumer must place the rescission notice in the mail, file it for telegraphic transmission, or deliver it to the creditor's place of business within that period in order to exercise the right.” A posting within the period is timely exercise even if it arrives after the deadline.

**5. Midnight.** The regulation fixes the end of the third business day, i.e., 11:59:59 p.m. on that day. The regulation does not specify a time zone; for a specific transaction this should be fixed by reference to the creditor's designated place of business and/or the consumer's location (see Part VII.D).

**6. Result stated as a value.** **3 business days** after the last triggering event, expiring at midnight of that third business day.

---

## V. Analysis of Ask 2 — the Extended-Expiration (Non-Delivery) Rule

**1. Condition predicate.** The second sentence is triggered only “if the required notice or material disclosures are **not delivered**.” It is a backstop for non-delivery, not an alternative measure of the ordinary period. If the notice or disclosures are delivered late but before any terminating event, the ordinary 3-business-day rule of Ask 1 applies and runs from the late delivery — the consumer is not thereby given 3 years.

**2. Three terminating events, earliest controls.** Where non-delivery persists, the right “shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, **whichever occurs first**.”

- **3 years after consummation** — a fixed anniversary date; the outer ceiling.
- **Transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property** — the consumer's own conveyance of the whole of his or her interest (e.g., a deed of the entire fee). A partial or fractional transfer does not, on the text, trigger this prong.
- **Sale of the property** — overlaps with the transfer prong but is independently sufficient, and captures a sale by someone other than the consumer (e.g., a senior lienholder's or tax sale), so the right dies with the sale even where the consumer did not formally convey.

**3. Practical statement.** The extended right can **never** be exercised more than 3 years after consummation, and will often die sooner. For a transaction consummated on 15 March of year Y, the outside date is 15 March of year Y+3, subject to earlier sale or transfer of all of the consumer's interest.

**4. Result stated as a value.** **3 years** after consummation (earliest of that date, transfer of all of the consumer's interest, or sale of the property).

---

## VI. Preconditions the Answers Assume (scope screen)

Both answers presuppose a transaction that is actually subject to § 1026.23. Before applying them:

1. **Security interest in the principal dwelling.** § 1026.23(a)(1) reaches a credit transaction in which a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in the **consumer's principal dwelling**, as to each consumer whose ownership interest is or will be subject to it. The addition of such a security interest to an existing obligation is itself a transaction, and the right applies only to the addition, not to the existing obligation; in that case only the (b) notice need be delivered, and delivery of the notice begins the period.
2. **Not exempt under § 1026.23(f).** Most importantly, **(f)(1)** exempts a “residential mortgage transaction” — i.e., purchase-money / initial-construction credit secured by the principal dwelling — so **no right of rescission arises at all** and neither answer applies. **(f)(2)** limits the right on a same-creditor refinancing to the new money.
3. **Open-end credit is elsewhere.** A home-equity line of credit secured by the principal dwelling is governed by § 1026.15, not § 1026.23. The parallel timing provisions of § 1026.15 should be confirmed separately; this memo does not opine on them.
4. **Waiver.** Under § 1026.23(e) the consumer may modify or waive the right on a dated written statement describing a bona fide personal financial emergency, signed by all consumers entitled to rescind; printed forms for the purpose are prohibited. A valid waiver ends the right.
5. **Assignees, damages and rescission mechanics** (§ 1026.23(d), § 1641) are outside this opinion.

---

## VII. Caveats and Items to Verify Before Reliance in a Live Matter

**A. § 125(f) administrative-proceeding extension.** The third sentence of (a)(3)(i) cross-refers to § 125(f) of the Act (15 U.S.C. § 1635(f)). The text of § 1635(f) is **not** among the fetched sources and I do not state its content. Read it directly in any matter involving a declaratory action by a creditor or assignee. It operates to **extend**, not shorten, the Ask 1 period; it does not alter either numeric answer as a general rule.

**B. “Business day.”** The definition sits in § 1026.2(a)(6) (a day on which the creditor's offices are open to the public for carrying out substantially all of its business functions) and was not among the fetched passages. It controls the Ask 1 count and the Saturday dependency identified in Part IV.3. Verify it and the creditor's actual hours.

**C. State law.** TILA § 1610 preemption and the § 1633 exemption procedure mean some states impose longer rescission rights. This memo states the **federal** rule only; it is not a ceiling on state-granted protection.

**D. Time zone of “midnight.”** Not specified in the regulation; fix it transaction-specifically.

**E. Case law (not among the fetched sources; verify before citing).** The Supreme Court has treated the 3-year period as a firm outer limit not subject to equitable tolling — *Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc.*, 575 U.S. 757 (2015). Cited here only as a pointer, not as a sourced holding of this memo.

**F. What this memo does not decide.** Whether any particular transaction is covered; whether any particular document satisfied “delivery” of the notice or of all material disclosures; whether a given conveyance was a “transfer of all of the consumer's interest” or a “sale”; and any limitations-period, damages, or class issues.

---

## VIII. One-Line Operational Rules

- **Ordinary case:** deadline = midnight of the 3rd business day after the later of {consummation, (b)-notice delivery, all-material-disclosures delivery}.
- **Non-delivery case:** deadline = the earliest of {consummation + 3 years, transfer of all of the consumer's interest, sale of the property}.
- **Exercise is complete on mailing / filing for telegraphic transmission / delivery to the creditor's designated place of business, whichever applies.**

---

## IX. Consistency Check on Stated Numbers

- **3 business days** (Ask 1) and **3 years** (Ask 2) are both quoted verbatim from § 1026.23(a)(3)(i); neither is derived.
- The 3-year figure is stated only as a **maximum** (“whichever occurs first”), never as an available period, so no downstream reader can treat it as a floor.
- The worked examples in Part IV.3 are reproduced from the official interpretation and are internally consistent with the stated counting convention (exclude the triggering day; count business days) **only** if the Saturday counts as a business day; the memo states that dependency explicitly rather than asserting a count that would conflict with the interpretation.
- No figure in the memo exceeds a bound the memo itself sets.

---

## X. Sources (all fetched 2026-11-23T12:03:49Z; operative language identical across all five)

1. eCFR, 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23 (current) — sha256 5e060cc324e9
2. CFPB, Regulations § 1026.23 — sha256 eb7886a55d84
3. CFPB, § 1026.23 snapshot 2026-04-08 — sha256 80ff8c8f615e
4. GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 12 vol. 9 § 1026.23 — sha256 b9c3107bd606
5. Federal Reserve, Regulation Z § 1026.23 — sha256 43b88f2cdeba

**Version note:** because all five snapshots (including the current eCFR and the 2026-04-08 CFPB version) carry identical operative text for (a)(3)(i), the choice of version does not change either answer.

answer:
# Right of Rescission Under 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i): Termination of the Right

## I. Questions presented and short answers

**Q1 (ask 2). Until when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction?**

Until **midnight of the third business day** following the **last** to occur of three events: (1) consummation of the transaction; (2) delivery of the notice of the right to rescind required by § 1026.23(b); (3) delivery of all material disclosures.

**Q2 (ask 3). When does the right expire if the required notice or material disclosures are never delivered?**

The right expires **3 years after consummation**, or **upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property**, or **upon sale of the property**, **whichever occurs first**.

## II. Controlling text

12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) (current text, as published at eCFR and in the 2026 print edition of 12 C.F.R. vol. 9; the two sources are word-for-word identical):

> "(3)(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act."

12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) (definition of the third trigger):

> "For purposes of this paragraph (a)(3), the term 'material disclosures' means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g)."

Note that the § 1026.23(b) notice is **not** a "material disclosure" under (a)(3)(ii). It is a **separate and independent trigger**. Both the notice and the material disclosures must be delivered before the three-business-day clock can run from the last of them.

## III. Element-by-element analysis

### A. The three trigger events

**1. Consummation.** Consummation is "the time that a consumer becomes contractually obligated on a credit transaction" (§ 1026.2(a)(13)). It is a single date, fixed by the contract, not by funding or recording.

**2. Delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice.** The notice must disclose, at a minimum: the security interest retained or acquired in the principal dwelling; the consumer's right to rescind; how to exercise it (with a form designating the creditor's business address); the effects of rescission; and **the date the rescission period expires** (§ 1026.23(b)(1)(i)–(v)). It must be on the Appendix H model form or a substantially similar notice (§ 1026.23(b)(2)). A defective notice — for example, one omitting the expiration date or the effects of rescission — is treated as not delivered, which puts the transaction into the extended period in Q2.

**3. Delivery of all material disclosures.** The closed list in (a)(3)(ii): APR, finance charge, amount financed, total of payments, payment schedule, plus the disclosures and limitations in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) (high-cost mortgages) and § 1026.43(g) (certain qualified mortgages). If any item is missing, materially inaccurate beyond the § 1026.23(g) tolerance, or delivered after consummation, the extended period governs until it is cured by actual delivery.

**4. The "whichever occurs last" rule.** The three-business-day clock starts only when all three have happened. The Bureau's official interpretation (comment 23(a)(3)-1.i) states the period "runs for 3 business days from the last of 3 events," and comment 23(b)(1)-4 gives the operative consequence: a notice delivered after consummation does not shorten the period — "the rescission period will not begin to run until the notice is given."

**5. Special case — adding a security interest to an existing obligation.** Under § 1026.23(a)(1), the addition of a lien on the principal dwelling to an existing debt is itself a rescindable transaction, but the creditor "need not deliver new material disclosures," and "[d]elivery of the required notice shall begin the rescission period." In that case the notice date alone starts the clock.

### B. Counting the three business days

**Definition.** § 1026.2(a)(6) contains two definitions. The general one ("a day on which the creditor's offices are open to the public for carrying on substantially all of its business functions") does **not** govern rescission. The second sentence of § 1026.2(a)(6) supplies a rescission-specific definition for §§ 1026.15 and 1026.23: **all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a)** (New Year's Day, MLK Day, Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas). Under that definition **Saturdays count as business days** even if the creditor is closed, and a weekday counts even if the creditor's offices are shut.

**Self-verification against the Bureau's own examples.** § 1026.2(a)(6) is not among the passages fetched for this matter, so the counting rule is confirmed arithmetically from the regulation's own worked examples (comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii):

- Consummation Friday, June 1; notice and disclosures delivered Thursday, May 31 → the last event is June 1. Deadline stated: **midnight Tuesday, June 5**. Check: Sat. June 2 = business day 1; Sun. June 3 excluded; Mon. June 4 = 2; Tue. June 5 = 3. ✔ This result is arithmetically impossible unless Saturday counts, which confirms the rescission-specific definition.
- Disclosures and consummation Friday, June 1; notice delivered Monday, June 4 → deadline **midnight Thursday, June 7**. Check: Tue. June 5 = 1; Wed. June 6 = 2; Thu. June 7 = 3. ✔

**Method.** Do not count the trigger day. Day 1 is the next day that is a business day under the rescission definition. The deadline is **midnight** of the third business day, not the close of the creditor's business.

**Exercise.** Under § 1026.23(a)(2), notice of rescission "is considered given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business." A consumer who deposits written notice in the mail before midnight on the third business day has timely exercised the right, even though the creditor receives it days later. Under § 1026.23(a)(4), rescission by one consumer is effective as to all consumers.

### C. The extended (three-year) period

**Trigger.** It applies only if "the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered" — that is, never delivered, or delivered in a form or at a time that does not count as delivery.

**Endpoints — earliest governs.**

1. **3 years after consummation.** Measured from the consummation date, not from discovery of the violation and not from the date the consumer learns of the disclosure failure. *Beach v. Ocwen Federal Bank*, 523 U.S. 410 (1998), construes 15 U.S.C. § 1635(f) as a statute of repose that fully extinguishes the right; it is not a limitations period subject to tolling or equitable modification.
2. **Transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property.**
3. **Sale of the property.**

**No suit required inside the three years.** *Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc.*, 575 U.S. 343 (2015): a borrower exercises the right by giving written notice within the three-year period; she need not file suit within that period. Written notice timely mailed is sufficient.

**Cure cuts the period back down.** If the notice or the material disclosures are delivered inside the three-year window, the extended period is displaced: the consumer then has the ordinary three business days measured from that late delivery (subject to the sale/transfer cutoffs, which are absolute).

**Administrative proceedings.** The final sentence of (a)(3)(i) cross-references § 125(f) of the Truth in Lending Act (15 U.S.C. § 1635(f)), under which the rescission period is extended in certain administrative enforcement proceedings.

### D. Related provisions that bound the answer

- **Coverage.** The right exists only where a security interest "is or will be retained or acquired in a consumer's principal dwelling" and the consumer holds an ownership interest subject to it (§ 1026.23(a)(1)).
- **Exempt transactions (§ 1026.23(f)).** No right of rescission for: a residential mortgage transaction (purchase-money); a refinancing or consolidation by the same creditor of debt already secured by the dwelling (except as to new money above the unpaid principal balance, earned unpaid finance charge, and refinancing costs); a transaction in which a state agency is the creditor; later advances in a series treated as a single transaction under § 1026.17(c)(6) where the notice and material disclosures were given; and renewal of optional insurance premiums not treated as a refinancing under § 1026.20(a)(5).
- **No performance during the period (§ 1026.23(c)).** No money may be disbursed other than in escrow, no services performed, and no materials delivered until the period has expired and the creditor is reasonably satisfied the consumer has not rescinded. Comment 23(c)-4 permits the creditor to wait a reasonable time after expiration for mailed notice, or to obtain a written statement that the right was not exercised.
- **Waiver (§ 1026.23(e))** only on the consumer's written, dated, post-consummation request in a personal financial emergency.
- **Open-end credit** is governed by the parallel rule in § 1026.15(a)(3), not § 1026.23.
- **Record retention.** § 1026.25(c)(1) sets a two-year minimum for evidence of compliance; because rescission exposure runs three years (plus the sale/transfer tail), the practical retention period for the notice, the disclosure package, and delivery evidence should be at least three years past consummation, and longer where litigation is anticipated.

## IV. Computation procedure

**Step 1 — Confirm coverage.** Security interest in the consumer's principal dwelling; consumer holds an ownership interest subject to it; transaction is not within § 1026.23(f). If not covered, no rescission period exists and the analysis ends.

**Step 2 — Fix the three dates.**
- C = consummation date (§ 1026.2(a)(13)).
- N = date the § 1026.23(b) notice was actually delivered to the consumer, or "never."
- M = date all material disclosures (the (a)(3)(ii) list) were actually delivered, or "never."

**Step 3 — Ordinary case (N and M both occurred).**
- T = the latest of C, N, M.
- Deadline = midnight of the third business day after T, counting with the § 1026.2(a)(6) rescission definition (exclude Sundays and 5 U.S.C. § 6103(a) holidays; include Saturdays; exclude T itself from the count).
- Record that date in the § 1026.23(b)(1)(v) field of the notice.

**Step 4 — Extended case (N or M never occurred, or delivery was defective beyond tolerance).**
- Deadline = the **earliest** of: (a) the third anniversary of C; (b) the date all of the consumer's interest in the property is transferred; (c) the date the property is sold.

**Step 5 — Operations.** Hold disbursement until the Step 3 or Step 4 date has passed and the creditor is reasonably satisfied no rescission was mailed (§ 1026.23(c); comment 23(c)-4). Calendar a post-expiration mail window (three to five days is typical practice) before releasing funds.

## V. Worked examples

**Example 1 (regulation's own).** C = Friday, June 1; N and M = Thursday, May 31. Last event = June 1. Deadline: **midnight Tuesday, June 5** (Sat. 6/2 = 1; Mon. 6/4 = 2; Tue. 6/5 = 3).

**Example 2 (regulation's own).** C and M = Friday, June 1; N = Monday, June 4. Deadline: **midnight Thursday, June 7** (Tue. 6/5 = 1; Wed. 6/6 = 2; Thu. 6/7 = 3).

**Example 3 (Saturday trigger).** C, N and M all Saturday, March 2, 2024. Sat. 3/2 is excluded as the trigger day; Sunday 3/3 is excluded; Mon. 3/4 = 1; Tue. 3/5 = 2; Wed. 3/6 = 3. Deadline: **midnight Wednesday, March 6, 2024**.

**Example 4 (federal holiday).** C, N and M all Wednesday, July 3, 2024. Thu. 7/4 (Independence Day) excluded; Fri. 7/5 = 1; Mon. 7/8 = 2; Tue. 7/9 = 3. Deadline: **midnight Tuesday, July 9, 2024**.

**Example 5 (notice never delivered).** C and M = March 1, 2020; N = never. The consumer still owns the home and has not transferred any interest. The right expires **March 1, 2023** — the third anniversary of consummation — and is extinguished on that date under *Beach*, with no tolling for discovery.

**Example 6 (late cure inside the window).** C and M = March 1, 2020; N delivered Tuesday, January 10, 2023. The extended period is displaced by the late delivery. Wed. 1/11 = 1; Thu. 1/12 = 2; Fri. 1/13 = 3. Deadline: **midnight Friday, January 13, 2023**. Had the property been sold in 2021, the right would instead have expired on the sale date, which is earlier and therefore controlling.

## VI. Common errors this analysis is designed to catch

1. Applying the general "creditor's offices are open" business-day definition to rescission. It is the wrong definition; under the rescission definition Saturdays count and a weekday holiday does not. (See the arithmetic proof in § III.B.)
2. Counting the trigger day as business day 1.
3. Treating "close of business" as the deadline. It is midnight.
4. Treating the § 1026.23(b) notice as one of the "material disclosures." It is a separate trigger, and the definition in (a)(3)(ii) does not include it.
5. Assuming the three-year period is tolled by the consumer's discovery of the violation. It is not (*Beach*).
6. Assuming the consumer must sue within three years. She need not (*Jesinoski*).
7. Overlooking the sale/transfer cutoffs, which can extinguish the right long before the third anniversary.
8. Overlooking the § 1026.23(f) exemptions, which can mean there is no rescission right at all.
9. Failing to restate the extended period after a late cure — once the notice or disclosures are actually delivered, only three business days remain.

## VII. Scope

This is the federal Regulation Z answer, current as of the eCFR text fetched 2026-11-23. State law may extend the rescission period or add independent grounds, and circuit authority varies on the mechanics of tender and on what constitutes a "transfer" or "sale" for the cutoff. Section 1026.2(a)(6) is not among the passages fetched for this matter; the rescission-specific definition stated in § III.B is the currently published text, and the counting rule it produces is independently confirmed by the two Bureau worked examples quoted above.

answer:
MEMORANDUM

To: File / Client
From: Legal Counsel
Re: Right of rescission under 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) — the exercise window and the expiration date where the rescission notice or material disclosures are never delivered
Regulatory text reviewed: 12 C.F.R. § 1026.23 as published on eCFR, on the CFPB's Regulation Z site (2026-04-08 edition), and in the 2026 and 2025 printed CFR volumes (sources fetched 2026-11-23).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(1) [Constraint] What rule does § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) impose — i.e., what is the operative legal constraint on the length of the rescission period that the answer must apply?
(2) [Value] Until when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction?
(3) [Value] When does that right expire if the required notice or the material disclosures are never delivered?

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. SHORT ANSWERS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(2) Until midnight of the third business day following the LAST to occur of three events: (a) consummation of the transaction; (b) delivery of the rescission notice required by § 1026.23(b); or (c) delivery of all material disclosures. The trigger is the last of the three, not consummation alone. The day of the triggering event is not counted; counting begins the next day; Saturdays count as business days, Sundays and federal legal holidays do not.

(3) The right expires on the EARLIEST of: (a) 3 years after consummation; (b) transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property; or (c) sale of the property. This is a calendar computation (no business-day adjustment), and it is an outer limit — not a substitute for the three-business-day window in (2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. GOVERNING TEXT (VERBATIM)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
12 C.F.R. § 1026.23(a)(3):

 "(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act.
  (ii) For purposes of this paragraph (a)(3), the term 'material disclosures' means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g)."

Exercise mechanics, § 1026.23(a)(2) (same section, as printed in the 2025 CFR volume):

 "To exercise the right to rescind, the consumer shall notify the creditor of the rescission by mail, telegram or other means of written communication. Notice is considered given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business."

Official interpretation, Comment 23(a)(3)-1 (rescission period):

 "i. The period within which the consumer may exercise the right to rescind runs for 3 business days from the last of 3 events: A. Consummation of the transaction. B. Delivery of all material disclosures. C. Delivery to the consumer of the required rescission notice.
  ii. For example: A. If a transaction is consummated on Friday, June 1, and the disclosures and notice of the right to rescind were given on Thursday, May 31, the rescission period will expire at midnight of the third business day after June 1 — that is, Tuesday, June 5. B. If the disclosures are given and the transaction consummated on Friday, June 1, and the rescission notice is given on Monday, June 4, the rescission period expires at midnight of the third business day after June 4 — that is, Thursday, June 7. The consumer must place the rescission notice in the mail, file it for telegraphic transmission, or deliver it to the creditor's place of business within that period in order to exercise the right."

4. ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.1 Two distinct clocks, one outer limit.
Section 1026.23(a)(3)(i) contains two rules, and the answer to (2) and the answer to (3) are governed by different clauses of the same sentence structure:
  - First sentence — the ordinary exercise window: three business days measured from the last of three events. This is the period the consumer is normally told about in the § 1026.23(b)(1)(v) notice ("[t]he date the rescission period expires").
  - Second sentence — the fallback/outer limit that applies when the notice or material disclosures are not delivered: three years from consummation, cut short by transfer of all the consumer's interest or by sale of the property.
The two clauses are not alternatives the creditor may pick between. The three-business-day window is the operative deadline whenever the notice and all material disclosures have been delivered; the three-year clause operates when delivery has not occurred (and, in practice, is treated as an absolute backstop in every case).

4.2 Trigger for the three-business-day window is the LAST of three events.
The three events are (i) consummation, (ii) delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice of the right to rescind, and (iii) delivery of all material disclosures. Whichever occurs last starts the clock. Comment 23(a)(3)-1 confirms the ordering, and Comment 23(b)-4 confirms that the notice need not precede consummation: "if the creditor provides the notice on May 15, but disclosures were given and the transaction was consummated on May 10, the 3-business-day rescission period will run from May 15." A late notice therefore restarts (not extends) the three-business-day clock — but it cannot push the consumer past the three-year backstop described in 4.5.

4.3 Counting the three business days (procedure an engineer can implement directly).
Inputs: C = consummation date; N = date the § 1026.23(b) notice was delivered (null if never delivered); M = date all material disclosures were delivered (null if never delivered).

Step 1. If N and M are both non-null: T = max(C, N, M). Go to Step 2.
Step 2. Set d = T + 1 calendar day. (The triggering day itself is never counted — Comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii.A.)
Step 3. Test d: it is a business day unless it is a Sunday or a legal public holiday listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a). Saturdays ARE business days for rescission purposes.
Step 4. If d is a business day, increment the counter; otherwise skip it.
Step 5. Repeat Steps 3–4 until the counter reaches 3. That date is the deadline; the right is exercisable until midnight at the end of that date.
Step 6. Exercise is complete if the consumer mails the notice, files it for telegraphic transmission, or delivers it to the creditor's designated place of business on or before that deadline (§ 1026.23(a)(2); Comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii.B).

Worked checks against the official interpretation (both reproduce the comment exactly):
  - Example A: C = Fri Jun 1; N and M = Thu May 31. T = Jun 1. Sat Jun 2 = day 1; Sun Jun 3 = excluded; Mon Jun 4 = day 2; Tue Jun 5 = day 3. Deadline: midnight, Tue Jun 5. ✔
  - Example B: C = Fri Jun 1; M = Jun 1; N = Mon Jun 4. T = Jun 4. Tue Jun 5 = day 1; Wed Jun 6 = day 2; Thu Jun 7 = day 3. Deadline: midnight, Thu Jun 7. ✔
  - Holiday illustration: T = a Friday, with a federal holiday falling on the following Monday. Sat = day 1; Sun excluded; Mon excluded (holiday); Tue = day 2; Wed = day 3. Deadline: midnight Wednesday.
The most common computational error is treating Saturday as a non-business day, which shortens the window by one day. The second most common is counting the triggering day itself.

4.4 What "business day" means here.
For rescission under §§ 1026.15 and 1026.23, "business day" is defined in § 1026.2(a)(6) as all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays specified in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) — a different definition from the "offices open to the public" test used elsewhere in Regulation Z. The § 1026.2(a)(6) text was not among the passages retrieved for this file, so it should be re-verified against the current eCFR before it is relied on in a contested matter. Two practical cautions: (a) the 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) list now includes Juneteenth National Independence Day; (b) where a listed holiday falls on a Saturday, confirm whether the observed Friday is treated as the holiday for rescission counting — conservative practice is to treat the observed date as a non-business day, which lengthens the consumer's window and is the safer assumption for a creditor computing its own compliance deadline.

4.5 Trigger for the three-year expiration (the "never delivered" branch).
If the required notice or the material disclosures are not delivered, the right "shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first." Three points of construction:
  (a) Three years after consummation is a calendar measure. There is no business-day adjustment and no exclusion of Sundays or holidays. Compute the third anniversary of the consummation date. (Because "expire 3 years after" is capable of being read as either the anniversary date or the day before it, treat the earlier of the two readings as the hard cut-off when advising a creditor on the last day it can safely ignore a rescission notice; treat the anniversary itself as the outer bound when advising a consumer.)
  (b) The three-year period is cut short by transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or by sale of the property, whichever happens first. These are events, not dates to be computed; a mid-period conveyance ends the right even though three years have not run.
  (c) Note the slight textual divergence between regulation and statute: the regulation adds "transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property" to the statutory trigger, which speaks of sale of the property (15 U.S.C. § 1635(f)). A partial transfer, or a transfer in which the consumer retains the ownership interest that is subject to the security instrument, does not obviously satisfy "all of the consumer's interest" — that question is fact-specific and courts have not read it uniformly.

Illustration: consummation on 2024-03-15, with neither the notice nor the material disclosures ever delivered and no transfer or sale. The right expires on 2027-03-15 (third anniversary). If the consumer conveys all of her interest on 2025-09-01, the right expires on 2025-09-01.

4.6 Which disclosures are "material" for this purpose.
Section 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) supplies a closed list: the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g). Failure to deliver any one item on that list keeps the three-business-day clock from starting and leaves the consumer in the three-year branch. Non-delivery of some other, non-material disclosure does not have that effect. Where a disclosure was delivered but is inaccurate, the tolerance provisions of § 1026.23(g) (one-half of 1 percent tolerance, subject to the exceptions in § 1026.23(g)(2)) and their commentary govern whether the disclosure counts as delivered; a variance outside tolerance can preserve the consumer's extended rescission rights, with the three-year limit operating as the backstop. Any specific transaction should be run against § 1026.23(g) and Supplement I rather than against this general rule.

4.7 Exercise versus expiration — the Jesinoski point.
Under § 1026.23(a)(2) the right is exercised by written communication, and notice is effective when mailed, filed for telegraphic transmission, or delivered to the creditor's designated place of business. The consumer does not have to file suit to rescind. In Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc., 574 U.S. 259 (2015), the Supreme Court held unanimously that rescission is effected by giving written notice within the statutory period and that a borrower need not sue within that period. The corollary for the three-year branch is that a written notice mailed on or before the expiration date is timely even if litigation follows years later — but a notice given after expiration is ineffective, because § 1635(f) has been treated as a statute of repose.

4.8 Adjacent provisions that change the answer in specific files.
  - Administrative proceedings: § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) extends the rescission period "in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act" (15 U.S.C. § 1635(f)) in certain administrative proceedings. The precise scope of that carve-out was not in the material retrieved for this file; confirm it against the statute before relying on it where a government enforcement action is involved.
  - Multiple consumers: § 1026.23(a)(4) — exercise by one consumer who has the right is effective as to all.
  - Waiver: § 1026.23(e) permits waiver only on a bona fide personal financial emergency; a valid waiver cuts off the right before the deadlines above.
  - Exempt transactions: § 1026.23(f) — residential mortgage transactions, refinancings/consolidations by the same creditor of debt already secured by the principal dwelling (except as to new money), transactions in which a state agency is the creditor, non-initial advances where notice and material disclosures were given, and renewals of optional insurance premiums. In these transactions no right arises, so the timing rules are moot; check (f) before doing any date arithmetic.
  - Open-end credit: § 1026.23 governs closed-end credit (Subpart C). Open-end credit is governed by § 1026.15, which contains a parallel timing rule at § 1026.15(a)(3). That section was not among the retrieved passages; if the file involves a HELOC, re-verify the § 1026.15 text rather than applying § 1026.23 by analogy.

4.9 Practical sequencing for a live file.
  1. Confirm the transaction is covered and not exempt under § 1026.23(f).
  2. Fix the consummation date from the closing documents.
  3. Fix the delivery dates for (i) the § 1026.23(b) notice and (ii) each item on the § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) material-disclosure list. If any item is missing, stop — go to the three-year branch.
  4. If everything was delivered, apply the counting procedure in 4.3 from the last delivery date.
  5. In every case, also compute the third anniversary of consummation and check for any transfer of all of the consumer's interest or sale of the property; the earliest of those three is the practical outer bound.
  6. Test whether the consumer's rescission notice was mailed, telegraphed, or delivered on or before that date (§ 1026.23(a)(2)).
